definitions.definition: A number in Einstein's equations that describes the energy density of empty space, which affects how fast the universe expands.
definitions.example: Think of it like a dial that controls how much the universe stretches. If it were turned up just a tiny bit, everything would fly apart too fast for stars to form.

definitions.definition: A number that determines how strongly charged particles like electrons interact with light and each other.
definitions.example: It's like the strength setting for the glue that holds atoms together. If it were different, atoms couldn't exist.

definitions.definition: A mathematical proof that any system of rules strong enough to do basic arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency using only its own rules.
definitions.example: Imagine a rulebook that says 'all rules in this book are true.' You can't prove that statement using only the rules in the book—you need something outside it.

definitions.definition: A proof that no system can define its own truth—you can't have a complete list of all true statements within the system itself.
definitions.example: Like trying to write a dictionary that defines every word, including the word 'dictionary'—you'd need an outside reference.

definitions.definition: A proof that no computer program can predict whether any other program will eventually stop or run forever.
definitions.example: You can't write a perfect 'stopwatch' app that tells you if any app will crash or finish—it's mathematically impossible.

definitions.definition: The law that says disorder (entropy) in a closed system always increases over time; things naturally fall apart unless energy is added from outside.
definitions.example: Your room gets messier on its own, but it never gets cleaner without you cleaning it.

definitions.definition: A rule that says erasing information always releases a tiny amount of heat, so computing has a minimum energy cost.
definitions.example: Every time you delete a file on your computer, a tiny bit of heat is produced—you can't get rid of information for free.

definitions.definition: Something that must exist and cannot not exist; it depends on nothing else for its existence.
definitions.example: A triangle's three sides are necessary for it to be a triangle—you can't have a triangle without them.

definitions.definition: Something that exists by its own nature and doesn't need anything else to cause it or keep it going.
definitions.example: Unlike a plant that needs soil and water, a self-existent thing just is—it doesn't rely on anything else.

definitions.definition: An endless chain of causes where each thing is caused by something before it, with no starting point.
definitions.example: If every book is written by an earlier author, you'd never find the first author—that's an infinite regress.

definitions.definition: The quality of being logically consistent, orderly, and fitting together in a unified way.
definitions.example: A good story where all the details match up and make sense has coherence.

definitions.definition: A set of symbols and rules for manipulating them, like a language or a computer program, used to prove statements.
definitions.example: Chess is a formal system: you have pieces (symbols) and rules for moving them.

definitions.definition: A basic statement that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for building other truths.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A statement that has been proven to be true using logic and axioms.
definitions.example: The Pythagorean theorem (a² + b² = c²) is a proven rule about right triangles.

definitions.definition: The ultimate foundation or source that makes everything else exist and keeps it in existence.
definitions.example: Like the foundation of a house that supports the whole building, the ground of being supports all of reality.

definitions.definition: Trust or confidence in something based on evidence, but going beyond what can be strictly proven.
definitions.example: You have faith in a friend when you trust them to keep a promise, even though you can't prove they will.
